title: Lazy Evaluation
summary: Deferring computation until its result is actually needed. Thunks and infinite structures show what laziness buys you; space leaks show what it costs when a chain of unevaluated work piles up instead of running.

slides.markdown:
**Strict (eager) evaluation** computes a value the moment it's bound. **Lazy evaluation** defers that computation until the value is actually *demanded* — read, printed, pattern-matched — and never runs it at all if it never is.

This single choice unlocks things eager languages can't express directly: an infinite list you can still work with, because you only ever force the prefix you actually consume; and a huge computation chain that runs in constant memory, because each step's result is produced and consumed immediately instead of materializing the whole intermediate collection.

The trade-off is real, though — laziness can quietly build up a chain of deferred work instead of running it, and that chain itself costs memory. This topic covers both sides: what laziness buys you, and the specific way it bites back if you're not careful.

slides.sectionTitle: Strict vs. lazy: compute now vs. compute on demand
slides.markdown:
Under **strict evaluation** — the default in Python, JavaScript, Java, most mainstream languages — `let x = expensive_computation()` runs `expensive_computation` immediately, right there, whether or not `x` ever gets used afterward.

Under **lazy evaluation**, the same line creates a placeholder — a **thunk** — that knows how to compute the value but hasn't yet. The actual computation only happens the first time something *forces* the thunk: reads its value, pattern-matches on it, prints it. If `x` is never touched, `expensive_computation` never runs at all.

Haskell is lazy by default for essentially everything — every binding is a thunk until forced. This isn't a performance trick bolted onto the language; it's the evaluation model the whole language is built around, which is why Haskell programmers can write things (like the infinite list on the next slide) that would need special-casing anywhere else.

slides.sectionTitle: A lazy list resolving one thunk at a time
slides.markdown:
The picture for how a lazy list gets consumed: nothing is computed ahead of where you've actually asked.

![A lazy list where only the first two elements are evaluated and the rest remain thunks or unevaluated tail](assets/lazy-list-forcing.svg)

Each element past what's been consumed stays a thunk — a description of "how to compute the next one," not an actual value — until something demands it. `take(3)` on this list forces exactly the first three thunks and leaves everything after them completely unevaluated, which is why the list can be infinite without ever causing a problem: you never force more of it than you ask for.

assets.alt: A lazy list where only the first two elements are evaluated and the rest remain thunks or unevaluated tail

slides.markdown:
Only lazy evaluation lets you write this and have it mean something useful, instead of hanging forever:

```haskell
naturals :: [Integer]
naturals = [0..]              -- an infinite list of every natural number

firstFive :: [Integer]
firstFive = take 5 naturals   -- [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]
```

`naturals` is genuinely infinite — there is no largest element, and defining it doesn't compute a single one of them. `take 5 naturals` forces exactly five elements of that infinite structure and stops; the rest is never touched, never allocated, never computed. Under strict evaluation, `naturals` itself would have to fully materialize before `take 5` could even be called — which is impossible for an infinite list, so the strict version of this program simply cannot be written this way at all; you'd need a generator or a manually bounded loop instead.

slides.sectionTitle: Where mainstream languages already have laziness
slides.markdown:
You don't need Haskell to use lazy evaluation — most mainstream languages have an opt-in mechanism for exactly this:

- **Python generators** — `def naturals(): n = 0; while True: yield n; n += 1` produces values one at a time on demand; `itertools.islice(naturals(), 5)` takes five without the generator ever running past that point.
- **Java Streams** — `Stream.iterate(0, n -> n + 1).limit(5)` is the same idea: the stream is a description of how to produce values, evaluated lazily element by element as the terminal operation (`limit`, `collect`) pulls from it.
- **JavaScript generators** — `function* naturals() { let n = 0; while (true) yield n++; }`, consumed with a `for...of` loop that stops whenever you `break`.

The difference from Haskell: these are all **opt-in** — you write `yield` or call `Stream.iterate` deliberately, and everything else in the language stays eagerly evaluated by default. Haskell's laziness is the default for everything, which is a meaningfully different design decision with its own trade-offs (the next few slides get into exactly what those are).

A thunk that's forced isn't recomputed on every subsequent access — most lazy implementations **memoize** it the first time it's evaluated, overwriting the thunk with the actual computed value so later reads are free.

This matters more than it sounds: without memoization, a value referenced from three different places in a lazy chain would get recomputed three separate times, once per access, silently multiplying the cost of anything expensive. With it, the first access pays the full cost and every access after that is just a memory read — the thunk becomes, in effect, a self-updating cache that fills itself in exactly once, on first demand.

This is also precisely why laziness composes so well with the [memoization use case for closures](closures-and-lexical-scope) — a lazy value *is* a closure over "how to compute this," plus a memoization slot for the result, packaged as one language primitive instead of something you build by hand.

slides.sectionTitle: Space leaks: thunks piling up instead of running
slides.markdown:
The classic lazy-evaluation footgun: building up a long chain of *unevaluated* thunks instead of actually running the computation as you go, then forcing the whole chain at once at the end.

A textbook case in Haskell: `foldl (+) 0 [1..1000000]` looks like it computes a running sum, but with a naive `foldl`, it actually builds a thunk like `((((0 + 1) + 2) + 3) + ... + 1000000)` — a million-deep nested, unevaluated expression — and only starts *evaluating* any of it when the final result is finally demanded. That forcing then has to unwind the entire million-deep chain in one go, which can blow the stack or spike memory far beyond what the computation should ever need.

The fix in this specific case is `foldl'` (strict fold), which forces each intermediate sum immediately instead of deferring it — turning the pile-up into genuine constant-space, step-by-step work. The general lesson: laziness defers work, it doesn't eliminate it, and a long enough chain of deferred work is itself a real cost sitting in memory until something forces it.

Haskell's model and mainstream languages' model solve the same problem with a very different default:

| | Haskell (default lazy) | Python/Java/JS (opt-in via generators/streams) |
|---|---|---|
| What's lazy by default | everything — every binding is a thunk | nothing — only what you explicitly write as a generator/stream |
| Infinite structures | natural, first-class (`[0..]`) | possible, but must be deliberately written as a generator |
| Space-leak risk | pervasive — any accidental thunk buildup anywhere in the program | localized — only inside the generator/stream code you wrote |
| Reasoning about performance | harder — you often can't tell when something runs just by reading the code | easier — eager code runs where it's written; lazy code is visibly marked (`yield`, `Stream`) |
| Debugging | lazy-evaluation bugs (wrong order, unexpected non-termination) show up anywhere | confined to the specific generator/stream you're looking at |

The trade *is* the design decision: Haskell's pervasive laziness enables things like infinite data structures and control structures as ordinary functions (not special syntax), at the cost of harder-to-predict evaluation order everywhere. Mainstream languages trade that generality for laziness being an explicit, visible, opt-in choice.

slides.sectionTitle: Why a generator pipeline uses constant memory
slides.markdown:
"Why does this generator-based pipeline use constant memory on a huge input file?" is asking you to connect laziness directly to memory behavior, not just define it.

The mechanism: `(line.strip() for line in open(path) if line.strip())` doesn't read the file into memory — it's a generator expression, a description of how to produce the next matching line, evaluated one line at a time as something downstream pulls from it. Chain several of these — `filter` then `map` then another `filter` — and each element flows through *all* the stages before the next element is even read from disk, rather than each stage fully materializing its output before the next stage starts. At any instant, memory holds roughly one element's worth of in-flight data per stage, not the whole file.

Compare that to the eager version — `[line.strip() for line in open(path).readlines() if line.strip()]` — which reads the *entire file* into a list before doing anything else, and then builds a second full list for the filter. On a multi-gigabyte file, that's the difference between the program running fine and it running out of memory before it starts.

slides.sectionTitle: Deciding when laziness earns its keep
slides.markdown:
The practical signal for reaching for laziness in a mainstream language: you're processing something that might be **large, infinite, or expensive to produce**, and you don't need all of it — just a prefix, or you want to process it one element at a time without materializing the whole thing.

Streaming a huge file line by line, generating an infinite sequence and taking the first N that satisfy some condition, or building a data pipeline where an early stage might filter out most of the input (so producing the rest eagerly would be wasted work) — these are the shapes where a generator or lazy sequence pays for itself.

The signal *against* it: small, bounded collections where eager evaluation's simpler, more predictable execution order is worth more than the memory savings — forcing laziness onto a 50-element list adds indirection and makes evaluation order harder to reason about, for a memory saving that was never going to matter. As with most trade-offs in this group, laziness is a tool for a specific shape of problem, not a universal upgrade.
